text: The OSI model is a reference model — nobody ships a device with exactly seven distinct protocol layers. The protocol suite that actually powers the internet is TCP/IP, named after its two most important protocols, and it groups the same ideas into four layers instead of seven.

TCP/IP's Application layer collapses OSI's top three layers — Application, Presentation, and Session — into one, because in practice the same protocol, like HTTP, is usually doing all three jobs at once. Transport and Internet map closely to OSI's Transport and Network layers, and Network Access covers OSI's Data Link and Physical layers together.

At the Transport layer, almost everything uses TCP or UDP, and picking the right one is a real design decision. TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery — right for web browsing, email, and file transfer. UDP is connectionless and faster, with no delivery guarantee — right for DNS lookups, video streaming, and voice calls.

TCP establishes that reliable connection with a three-way handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client finishes with ACK. Only then does real data start flowing, and the connection stays tracked for the life of the conversation.

UDP skips all of that — it sends a datagram and moves on, which is exactly why it's the right choice for a live video call, where a dropped frame that arrives late is worse than one that's simply skipped.

You'll hear OSI and TCP/IP language mixed in the same sentence constantly in the field — OSI's seven layers for precise troubleshooting vocabulary, TCP/IP's four layers for how the real software stack is organized.
